top_picks.title: Plaster Wall Heights: That Extra 3 Inches Means More Money
top_picks.original_description: Don't leave money on the table. If you have plaster walls chances are your wall height is 8' 3". That extra 3" may not seem like a lot, but you can do the math in your head. 8' Ã 12" is 96". So a regular 8' wall is pretty close to 100". So that extra 3" is roughly 3%. Actually a tiny bit more than 3%. So let's say you have $10,000 worth of wall painting. 3% of that equals $300, before O&P and sales tax. So who is telling me that the price for an estimator should be a $350 flat fee? The 3" difference is almost equal to the low price estimator fee on just one measurement error on one line item.  Also, getting your measurements and your sketch correct gives a lot of credibility to the estimate. You can go round and round with subjective arguments all day long about whether something is high grade or low grade. But when you're negotiating with the insurance company or going to appraisal  and you can say that your measurements are accurate and the other person's measurements are not, that's not a subjective difference.

all_videos.original_description: Can we really trust our common sense to determine what evidence means? If you see some green mold is that conclusive evidence that the leak must be 2 months old? A lot of times we use our interpretation of Visual Evidence to decide that something happened a long time ago or happened recently but are we making wrong assumptions sometimes? On both sides of the fence in claims. Check out this very delicate spider web that survived historically heavy Southern California rain driving at 30 miles an hour. Anybody seeing this spiderweb the day after the rain would naturally assume it had been freshly made that morning or the night before. I never would have imagined a delicate spider web would survive even just one day of heavy rain. Or a 10 minute drive at 30 mph.

top_picks.title: Engineers Never Ask Witnesses: Physical Evidence vs Human Intelligence
top_picks.original_description:
I've been saying this forever. See this scene in a detective movie. They 1) revisit the crime scene, presumably to examine PHYSICAL EVIDENCE and 2) "chat up the neighbors", presumably to gather HUMAN INTELLIGENCE AKA EYEWITNESS TESTIMONY.

This is routine in investigations.

Unless it's an engineer doing an "investigation" for an insurance carrier. They do #1 but never #2.

They never ask anyone who witnessed the hail or the wind. They never ask the homeowner when repairs were done, before or after the wind event. They never ask when the shingles were last installed. They never ask about things that would corroborate the wind event like trash cans blowing down the street, trees falling over, and they don't ask about things that would corroborate hail like damaged vehicles. They just don't ever ask.

Why do detectives and police officers always do #1 and #2 but engineers only do #1?

The next best method is to use a redhead, one of these expansion bolts, they're supposed to go in 7 in but a lot of people use the shorter ones and as long as the building inspector doesn't see the Box they might get away with it because you can't tell from looking once it's installed. all_videos.original_description: When you test for asbestos you have to consider the roofing mastic, the VCT or vinyl floor tile, the mastic underneath the floor tile, additional layers of flooring, the joint compound in the drywall, and if the property was built and remodeled 6 or 7 times you might need to test in every different part of the structure to make sure you've identified every area. Look at this property in my video it probably was added onto 6 or 7 times.

top_picks.original_description: Matterport allows you to remove furniture from an image. top_picks.title: Xactimate Breakout: Practical Interior Estimating & Strategy
top_picks.original_description: Truth in Advertising- My "Xactimate" breakout session is more of a practical interior estimating/strategy class than an Xactimate certification type class. I will NOT teach anything that will help you get certified. If anything, I will teach some more beginner things and some hacks that have worked for me. You might leave my class knowing one or two strategies, line items, or methods of documenting something in the software that helps you make an extra $1000 to $30,000, maybe more, on an estimate. This will not be a substitute for the kind of class that Stephen Harmon teaches. I need to take his class myself.  I will try to share tips from my experience estimating for contractors, attorneys, other PAs, as an adjuster (9 years daily claims + many CATs worldwide), and more recently as a PA.  If you are torn between my breakout and another one at the same time you might want to take the other one because I will do my best to share my material in person or by email, whatever we can work out.
